title: Garfield Law: Inside the World's First AI-Native Law Firm — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Philip Young · Daniel Long

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source reframes automation primarily as an opportunity to improve associate development rather than as a threat to expertise reproduction. It predicts that juniors will assume higher-level work earlier and that large firms will adopt a small-firm-style training model, but it does not address how foundational expertise or verification ability will be deliberately developed once routine work disappears. These are forecasts, not measured training outcomes.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source does not assess whether automation weakens apprenticeship or partner-succession routes. It instead shifts attention to client-driven adoption, faster dispute resolution and expanded demand from previously uneconomic work, while flagging fabricated citations as an unresolved risk.

st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s client-driven adoption and demand-expansion theses, and materially extends them by forecasting faster dispute resolution through compression of routine procedural work. st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Garfield accepts the value of specialist, workflow-specific legal AI and materially extends the synthesis with a concrete AI-native delivery model: bounded small-debt litigation performed through a regulated law firm rather than software merely sold to lawyers. Its claims support targeted automation and regulated accountability, but provide product rationale rather than measured performance evidence.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s framing of AI adoption as workflow and service redesign and adds concrete implementation detail: connected accounting data, document-flow integration, and intensive scenario-based testing of branching claims workflows. st.an: Garfield accepts the cluster’s core view that value comes from redesigning bounded legal workflows within accountable, regulated systems rather than deploying a standalone tool. Its prediction of increased lawyer demand is speculative but does not displace the overall alignment.

kp.k: Regulated AI delivery targets small debt litigation
kp.d: Phillip Young describes Garfield as an English law firm delivering services through AI, pursuing small debt claims up to the edge of trial. He characterizes these matters as fact-heavy, procedurally intensive and usually legally uncomplicated. Daniel Long qualifies the apparent simplicity: the workflow has numerous branching pathways, although these eventually close off. Young claims jurisdictional priority and believes Garfield is the world's first such firm.
qs: we built this product called Garfield that now seeks to do what a good English law firm would do to pursue a small debt claim, all the way up to the edge of trial.
So essentially it's an English law firm that provides services through AI, which makes it a first in our jurisdiction and, I believe, the world.
Luckily, they do tend to close off eventually, which is what we mean by a closed problem space.

kp.k: Small-claim economics leave substantial legal needs unmet
kp.d: Young says small and medium businesses typically lack general counsel or substantial legal budgets and must pursue debts themselves or abandon recovery when external representation is uneconomic. He identifies manual work and the absence of ordinary loser-pays cost recovery in small claims as barriers, particularly for sums up to around £10,000. Citing unspecified surveys rather than presenting a study, he places annual uncollected small debt in England between £6 billion and north of £23 billion.
qs: But certainly for small debts (sums up to around £10,000), it's usually uneconomic to hire an external law firm.
although in England we have a different rule than you do about cost recovery (in England the general rule is the loser pays the winning side's legal costs), that rule doesn’t apply in small claims.
depending on which survey you read, each year anywhere between £6 billion and north of £23 billion of debt just isn't collected—that is, small debt in England.

kp.d: Young reports an eight-month approval process involving ethical and regulatory scrutiny. He attributes the SRA's willingness to approve Garfield to its access-to-justice duty, concerns about poorly prepared self-represented cases consuming judicial time, and risks from people using unregulated consumer LLMs in litigation. He also reports ongoing quarterly check-ins and feedback subject to confidentiality. McCormack's contrasting suggestion that US jurisdictions would not approve an equivalent soon is her assessment, not a regulatory finding.
qs: That process took eight months in total, which gave us a lot of time to line up some early adopters.
our regulator in England—the SRA (Solicitors Regulation Authority)—has a public duty to promote access to justice, and they take that really seriously.
Everyone's been very concerned about that and keen to get to a world where regulated products are available.
We're doing quarterly check-ins with them

kp.k: Professional accountability shaped the software architecture
kp.d: Young says the architecture incorporated duties to the court, confidentiality and conflicts from inception, rather than adding compliance after development. He identifies himself as the firm's Compliance Officer for Legal Practice, accountable to the regulator and judiciary for Garfield's functioning and ethical compliance. The host also introduces him as reviewing all platform outputs; the detailed discussion emphasizes his accountability without explaining that review workflow.
qs: In that role, he reviews all the platform’s outputs from Garfield Law—they'll tell us all about how Garfield works.
You have to consider what's called the Hamid obligation (the duty you owe to the court as a lawyer). You also have to maintain client confidentiality, deal with conflicts of interest
So we built the architecture of our software with all of that firmly in mind from day one.
So I'm accountable to my regulator, and I'm accountable to the judiciary, for the functioning of Garfield and its compliance with the ethical rules.

kp.k: Structured workflows enable monitoring and regulatory feedback
kp.d: Long says Garfield records users' positions and routes through the process, allowing user-journey reporting that he contrasts with the unstructured information in conventional firms. The team also uses LLMs to analyze possible failures, user intentions and opportunities for improvement. He expresses an intention to produce usage statistics, rather than presenting measured outcomes in the episode.
qs: But in our system, everything is tracked; we've discretized everything in terms of where users are and which routes they go down.
We even use LLMs themselves to figure out if something went wrong, what the user wanted to happen, and how the system could work better.
we'd like to produce some interesting stats about how people are using the platform—what’s working and what isn’t—in a way that would be hard without an AI-driven system.

kp.d: Young describes an existing County Court API integration that sends claim forms and documents and receives court data. Following pre-action correspondence and filing, Garfield supports payment, default judgment, admissions and defended claims, including telephone mediation and preparation for a small-claim trial. Resolution without attending court is conditional on not needing to appear before a judge; the service is not described as replacing judicial adjudication.
qs: Garfield is essentially integrated into the County Court service. Garfield can send claim forms to the court and other documents to the court, and it can receive data back from the court.
You might receive no response—in which case Garfield applies for default judgment (again a programmatic process that Garfield handles for you).
There's a compulsory mediation on that track as well, which Garfield will help you attend (it's by telephone).
Garfield handles all of those possible pathways a claim could take.

kp.k: Data integration reshapes firms beyond document generation
kp.d: Young reports current integrations with Companies House for debtor status, accounts and solvency assessment, and clients' accounting platforms for unpaid invoices. Over the next ten years he envisages firms becoming highly integrated data-exchanging businesses, with further court APIs, common standards and shared document environments. Land Registry integration is prospective; automated SMS and calls are announced for a couple of months after the interview, with controls against nuisance.
qs: Amazingly, where we're going to end up in the next ten years is a highly integrated kind of business that fundamentally exchanges data a lot more swiftly with all of the parties it deals with.
We're integrated with Companies House (our companies registry in England).
Garfield integrates with our users' accounting platforms, so you can pull unpaid invoices and data straight from their accounts.
Fairly soon we're going to roll out a service—and I don't mind telling you this is coming in just a couple of months—where Garfield can send automated SMS messages and make automated phone calls.
The English court system is trying to promote a common data standard, and I think that will drive a lot of this.

kp.k: Hybrid architecture constrains probabilistic model outputs
kp.d: Young attributes hallucination-risk reduction to a deterministic expert system controlling what LLM components can do. Long describes parallel LLMs extracting and modifying claim information, followed by traditional code checking conditions such as the £10,000 small-claim limit and limitation periods, rather than asking an LLM whether a claim is valid. These are the developers' descriptions of safeguards, not independently measured error rates.
qs: It has a deterministic expert system and a probabilistic LLM-based series of systems.
The expert system is deterministic, so we let it be in charge—that then controls the universe of possible things the LLM can or might do.
there are many LLMs running in parallel, determining how different parts of the claim should be modified based on the user's instructions.
we're actually using traditional flow control in our codebase to make sure conditions are met.

kp.k: User approval limits autonomous legal action
kp.d: Young says users see the system's interpretation of their documents and available next steps, can correct misunderstandings and must approve every action. He analogizes this to lawyers obtaining client approval and checking client-supplied facts. Long similarly stresses that users cannot assume correctness and disengage. This is an explicitly supervised service model, despite automated processing and filing.
qs: We tell the user at every stage what Garfield has understood from the documents they've uploaded and from the information it's been given.
And it's not autonomous—the user has to approve each action before the system takes it.
So you always need the client to check the facts.
the system is making their life easier, but we don’t let them take their hands off the wheel and assume everything will be correct.

kp.d: Long says only maybe 30–40% of development time went into building the product, with the majority spent testing. Alongside conventional input-output tests, LLM-simulated users with or without small debts exercise branching scenarios in parallel to identify classification and workflow problems. Young compares iterative AI document production to junior, senior and partner review in firms. The transcript provides no test sample sizes, pass rates or quantified hallucination results.
qs: We spent maybe 30–40% of our time building the actual product, but the majority of our time is spent testing the product.
we have Garfield talk to itself and pretend to be a user that has a small debt (or maybe doesn’t have one).
we realized we could actually use an LLM to simulate the system and run multiple scenarios in parallel. That allows us to flag issues really quickly.
a review–correction–iteration process is how law firms operate.

kp.k: Human competence anchors reported regulatory expectations
kp.d: Young reports that the SRA considered performance at least equivalent to a reasonably competent human sufficient. He also asserts that hallucinations appear to decline as models improve and anticipates specialist products addressing legal hallucinations within the next year or two. These are his reported regulatory conversations, observations and forecasts, not a quoted formal standard or demonstrated elimination of hallucinations.
qs: Certainly from the SRA's perspective, the point they made to me was: if our product is operating at least at the level of a reasonably competent human, that's already more than good enough.
And as models get better and better, the incidence of hallucinations does seem to drop dramatically.
They're going to be on the market in the next year or two.

kp.k: Lower delivery costs could expand lawyer demand
kp.d: Young predicts more lawyers will be needed as technology makes previously uneconomic transactions and litigation viable; additional claims would also generate defendant-side work. McCormack separately estimates that lawyers currently serve about 10% of the potential market. Long envisages disputes resolved in a month or two by compressing nonjudicial work while preserving judicial attention, with wider economic benefits. These are optimistic market and efficiency forecasts, not demonstrated Garfield outcomes.
qs: I think there's going to be a need for a lot more lawyers.
as that work is dealt with by technology, suddenly those transactions or cases are going to be economic to do, and therefore they will be pursued and lawyers are going to be engaged.
if a claimant decides to bring a claim they otherwise wouldn't have, that's going to be work for the defendant side as well.
Right now I think lawyers are only hunting in about 10% of the potential legal market
That could mean the whole economy benefits massively—where a legal dispute could be resolved in a matter of a month or two.

kp.k: Junior formation may shift toward higher-level practice
kp.d: Young predicts automation of document-intensive diligence and discovery will move junior lawyers earlier into client management, case strategy and legal argument. He contrasts large-firm document work with small-firm trainees' early responsibility, forecasting convergence toward the latter model. He also reports, without quantified evidence, that corporate general counsel are already pressing external firms to adopt AI aggressively to reduce legal spending.
qs: With this technology, even as a junior lawyer you'll be doing higher-level skills at a much earlier stage.

If you were a trainee at a small firm, you'd be thrown in the deep end on day one and expected to do higher-level things like manage clients and shape case strategy and come up with the best legal arguments.
I think even big firms are going to end up adopting a small-firm training model as a consequence of this technology.

We're already—even just two years into this—seeing lots of big companies' general counsels insisting that their external law firms take up AI (and take it up aggressively) to drive down the legal spend those companies have.

kp.k: Law firms adopt Garfield for economics and scale
kp.d: Young reports unexpectedly positive professional reception and says a sizable, unquantified share of users are law firms recovering their own or clients' debts, seeking more economical delivery, better margins and faster scaling. He attributes comfort partly to lawyer-technologist collaboration, SRA regulation and the unmet need addressed. He describes a cautious judicial welcome but explicitly distinguishes it from endorsement of a private product.
qs: When I look at the users on our platform so far, a sizable chunk of them are law firms—either pursuing their own debts or using Garfield to pursue their clients' debts in a way that's more economical for them, gives them more margin, and allows them to scale up faster as a firm.
They have cautiously welcomed this development as well—without, of course, endorsing it in any way, because they're judges and they can't endorse a private product.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Young and Long present Garfield as a regulated, AI-enabled small-debt practice and predict more integrated legal delivery, expanded demand for lawyers, earlier higher-level junior work, and faster dispute resolution.
pts.d:
1. Phillip Young says Garfield seeks to perform the work of a good English law firm pursuing a small debt up to the edge of trial, delivering services through AI under law-firm regulation. He claims jurisdictional first status and qualified worldwide first status. He describes small-debt work as fact-heavy, generally legally uncomplicated, and primarily procedural; Daniel Long qualifies that the process has many branching pathways, although these eventually close off. Young says Garfield handles pre-action correspondence, claim submission, default judgment applications, admissions, and preparation through mediation and contested proceedings; he does not claim it replaces the trial judge or represents clients autonomously at trial.
2. Young argues automation can make currently uneconomic small claims and transactions worth pursuing. He predicts more work and a need for more lawyers, rather than net professional displacement: newly viable claimant matters also generate defendant-side work. He describes existing law-firm users pursuing their own or clients' debts more economically, improving margins and scaling faster.
3. Young predicts firms will become highly integrated businesses exchanging data programmatically with courts, registries, clients' accounting systems, and other firms. He describes current County Court, Companies House, and accounting-platform integrations; predicts further court APIs and Land Registry integration; and anticipates shared document environments replacing cumbersome paper service and large emailed PDFs. He announces automated SMS and telephone capabilities as a forthcoming Garfield service.
4. Young predicts automation of document-intensive junior work will bring client management, strategy, and legal argument into junior lawyers' work earlier. He expects large firms to adopt training resembling small-firm practice, driven partly by corporate general counsels demanding AI adoption and lower external legal expenditure.
5. Long predicts acceleration of procedural work could enable disputes to resolve within a month or two, speed trials and appeals, and benefit economies adopting the technology, while preserving judges' time and attention for judgment.
6. Young and Long claim a hybrid architecture can constrain hallucinations and other errors: a deterministic expert system controls permissible actions while multiple LLMs extract and modify information. Transparent presentation of extracted facts, user corrections, approval of each action, iterative review, and testing are central safeguards. Young presents this as risk minimisation, not an autonomous LLM-only service. Long says converting the workflow into verifiable data and traditional flow control can prevent hallucinated outputs within that design.
7. Young says model improvements appear to reduce hallucinations and predicts dedicated legal-document hallucination-remediation products will reach the market. He also anticipates eventual superhuman capability, without specifying a date.
8. Long claims structured tracking makes user journeys and problems easier to monitor and report than in a typical firm with unstructured information. He describes LLM-assisted feedback analysis and simulated-user testing as ways to identify issues quickly across branching claim pathways.
9. Young expects further Garfield-like products, saying he has already seen others under development in England. He attributes Garfield's regulatory route to access-to-justice concerns, demand for regulated alternatives to consumer LLMs, compliance designed into the architecture, and accountable legal leadership. His account of judicial receptiveness expressly stops short of product endorsement.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The account primarily offers founders' implementation experience, practice experience, internal testing descriptions, and economic reasoning; it supplies no published performance benchmark or quantified outcome evaluation.
pts.d:
For claim 1, Young traces the idea to helping his plumber brother-in-law recover unpaid debts, his commercial-litigation experience, GPT-4's arrival, and roughly two years of development with Long and their team. He reports an eight-month regulatory approval process and quarterly regulator check-ins. The first-in-the-world description is his qualified assertion, not a documented comparative survey.
For claim 2, Young explains the economics through time-intensive manual work, low claim values, and the small-claims exception to ordinary loser-pays costs recovery. He cites unspecified surveys putting annually uncollected small debt in England between £6 billion and more than £23 billion. No survey names, dates, methods, or comparable definitions are supplied. Increased lawyer demand is an inference from making latent work economic, not an employment-data finding. Existing law-firm uptake is supported by his report that a sizable portion of users are firms; no counts, margins, savings, or recovery outcomes are given.
For claim 3, Young offers concrete descriptions of functioning integrations: sending and receiving court data, checking corporate debtors through Companies House, and pulling unpaid invoices from accounting platforms. His wider prediction rests on these experiences and his account of government API development and a court-system common-data-standard initiative, rather than measured interoperability gains.
For claim 4, Young relies on his comparison of small- and large-firm training and his observation that corporate general counsels already insist on AI adoption. He gives no named corporate examples or systematic training evidence.
For claim 5, Long explicitly identifies his position as techno-optimism. Faster resolution and economy-wide gains follow from a proposed compression of nonjudicial work; no trial-duration data or economic estimate is offered.
For claims 6–7, the evidence consists of architecture and safeguard descriptions, analogies with law-firm review and software testing, and Young's general observations about improving models. Young mentions unspecified online statistics and unnamed products he has recently seen. He reports a regulator's reasonably-competent-human standard, but provides no evaluation demonstrating Garfield's attainment of that standard. Long's stronger prevention language is not accompanied by a measured hallucination rate.
For claim 8, Long estimates that only 30–40% of development time went into building the product, with the majority spent testing. He describes conventional input-output tests and LLM-simulated users, including users without valid debts, run across multiple scenarios. These are descriptions of internal tests, not published benchmarking results; he presents user-journey statistics as something they would like to produce.
For claim 9, Young relies on direct regulatory experience, products shown to him, and reported reactions from practitioners and judges. Regulatory motivations and judicial attitudes are his account, not independently presented statements by those institutions.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current capabilities are distinguished from near-term product plans, a ten-year integration forecast, and undated predictions conditional on automation, infrastructure, regulation, and continued human involvement.
pts.d:
The episode is identified as 2025; all relative deadlines refer to the interview, whose exact date is not supplied. Garfield's described capabilities, law-firm uptake, tracking, safeguards, and testing are present-tense founder reports following approximately two years of development. Young links the project's origin to GPT-4 in March or April 2023.
The service is currently framed around English small-debt claims, with sums around £10,000 and work through the edge of trial. Long stresses that even this bounded domain is procedurally complex. Young's broader claims about larger litigation and transactional work are extrapolations, not descriptions of Garfield's established scope.
Young places the integrated-firm transformation within the next ten years. He describes further court APIs as coming, Land Registry integration as inevitable without a deadline, and automated SMS and calls as due in a couple of months, subject to controls against nuisance. He separately predicts that paper claim submission will cease in the next month or two; this is a contextual court-digitisation forecast, not an AI performance result. Common data standards and additional institutional APIs are enabling conditions for the wider integration vision.
The predictions of more lawyers, expanded viable work, and changed junior training have no precise delivery date. They depend on technology reducing low-value, time-intensive work and clients pressing firms to adopt it. Long's month-or-two dispute resolution is a possible future duration, not a deadline for rollout or a claim about current Garfield case outcomes; he conditions the benefit on accelerating tasks that do not require a judge while preserving deliberation.
The safety claims depend on deterministic constraints, bounded workflows, transparent extraction, correction, testing, and user approval. The service is expressly not autonomous, and Long acknowledges that mistakes may occur. Young's prediction of dedicated hallucination-remediation products is one to two years from the interview; his eventual-superhuman prediction is undated and conditional on technological progress.
Regulatory feasibility is discussed in the English framework, with continued accountability and quarterly supervision. Young's account does not establish equivalent permission in other jurisdictions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate beneficiaries described are small businesses with uneconomic unpaid debts and firms serving them; the predicted effects extend to defendants, junior lawyers, corporate legal buyers, courts, regulators, and the economy.
pts.d:
Small businesses and other small-debt claimants: Young describes an access-to-justice gap among people without in-house counsel, meaningful legal budgets, or confidence navigating court. AI-enabled process handling is intended to make enforcement affordable and manageable. Corporate-status and solvency checks can also help users avoid spending money on unrecoverable debts. Users remain responsible for checking facts and approving actions.
Defendants: Young predicts that additional claimant proceedings create additional defendant-side legal work. This is part of his demand-expansion argument, not a prediction that only claimants benefit.
Law firms and practising lawyers: Existing firms reportedly use Garfield both to recover their own unpaid bills and to serve clients more economically. Young expects improved margins and scalability in that segment and more legal work across newly viable disputes and transactions. Garfield is described as delivering regulated legal services, not merely selling software to lawyers.
Junior lawyers and large firms: Young expects less document-heavy drudgery and earlier responsibility for clients, strategy, and arguments. His small-firm-training comparison is about work and development, not a specified staffing shape or quantified change in associate-to-partner leverage.
Corporate general counsels and external firms: Young describes buyer-side pressure to use AI to reduce corporate legal expenditure. This enterprise-cost argument is distinct from the small-business access-to-justice claim.
Courts and judges: Better-prepared cases and programmatic information exchange are presented as responses to overloaded courts and the burdens of poorly prepared self-representation. Long expects procedural acceleration without sacrificing judicial attention; Young anticipates real-time access to shared case documents.
Regulators and accountable legal professionals: Structured journey reports and quarterly feedback may help develop oversight for later providers. Young emphasises his responsibility as Compliance Officer for Legal Practice to the regulator and judiciary, together with duties concerning confidentiality, conflicts, and the court.
The public and wider economy: Young frames regulated provision as an alternative to potentially inaccurate consumer-LLM legal assistance. Long predicts broad economic benefits from faster dispute resolution in adopting economies.
